Q23.text: I'm a late-stage graduate student, so my use of social media platforms is different than that of established PIs. I use Twitter and Facebook for sharing content, but also for learning about science that is OUTSIDE of my field. For example, by following the Scientific Reports twitter account, I saw an article and learned about plants responding to tactile stimuli. I'm a human physiology researcher, but the larger my breadth of knowledge, the more things I can draw upon for my future studies! These are things that I would not normally find by digging around on PubMed (which is also becoming a social site itself with comments, etc). Social media also serves to show me content that lots of people are talking about, particularly for hot topics like CRISPR. /  / In addition, I use social media for outreach. For over a year, I served as a social media manager for a fledgling public science outreach group that aimed to bring science from real scientists to middle and high school students though a variety of ways, but also to adults through science cafes. Our social media presence is why the group grew and later got absorbed by a larger outreach group, and I found that the public was actually seeking groups like us to learn from. People LIKE talking to scientists, but they don't know how to get to us, and are often intimidated because of the stigma behind being a scientist. They don't get that we're just normal people who do science. Social media is a highly effective platform to address science to the public, and it can be done in ways that are not intimidating to the public, but only if it is done correctly. That is something I'm happy to discuss if there is any way to link information. This makes social media highly important for my career as a scientist; so long as there is fear, miscommunication, and distance between scientists and the public, we're going to have a hard time moving forward. Thus, by being one of the people who tries to take science to nonscientists in a fun and inviting way, I'm helping my career and that of others... and having fun doing so!

Q23.text: Science communication is HUGE for me — I actually manage the social media accounts for a public science group, so I use Twitter and Facebook to actively engage the general public with research findings, not just other researchers. It goes well beyond sharing papers; we're talking about creating accessible content that reaches OUTSIDE the academic bubble to people who would never stumble across a journal article on their own. There is this incredible appetite out there for science that most researchers don't even realise exists, and honestly that's what drives me to keep posting even when it feels like a lot of work on top of the PhD. I also use it for interdisciplinary learning — following researchers in completely unrelated fields has genuinely shaped how I think about my own work in human physiology. you'd be surprised how much a thread on ecology or cognitive science can spark something totally unexpected in your own research!

Q37.text: Sharing professional content is where social media REALLY shines for me, and I think it's one of the most underutilised aspects by researchers who are still stuck in the "just email a PDF" mindset. When I share a paper or a summary of a finding on Twitter, it doesn't just reach the 12 people who subscribed to that journal's alert — it reaches curious people across disciplines, students who couldn't access the paywalled version, and honestly just members of the public who are genuinely interested and never knew this research existed. The reach is incomparable to anything traditional publishing offers. Facebook has been particularly useful for sharing longer-form content through our science group page, where we can actually have a conversation with people in the comments rather than just broadcasting into a void. I do think researchers undersell themselves here — there's sometimes this attitude that dumbing down for social media compromises your work, but I'd argue the opposite: learning to explain your research clearly enough for a general audience actually deepens your own understanding of it. The sharing piece is what gets science OUT of the ivory tower, and I genuinely dont think we leverage it anywhere near as much as we could.

Q43.text: Promotion is something I feel really strongly about because there's still this weird stigma in academia around "self-promotion" — like if you're actively pushing your work out into the world, you're somehow being immodest or unscholarly, which is honestly such an outdated attitude. If you've done good research, you have an OBLIGATION to make sure people know it exists! Twitter has been incredible for this — a well-crafted tweet about a new finding can generate more interest in 24 hours than a paper sitting in a journal for six months. And I don't just mean interest from other researchers; I mean journalists, policy people, educators, members of the public who might actually be affected by what you've found. That's the piece that excites me most. I've seen colleagues get media coverage and real-world uptake from research that would otherwise have been read by maybe 50 specialists, purely because they put the effort into communicating it accessibly on social media. The promotion angle also forces you to think about impact in a much more concrete way — who does this research matter to, and how do I reach them? I think it should honestly be part of every researcher's workflow, not treated as an optional extra you do if you happen to be a "social media person." We all need to be social media people now, whether we like it or not!

Q47.text: Networking is where I think social media has genuinely changed the landscape of academic collaboration in ways that would have been impossible even ten years ago. I've had direct conversations on Twitter with researchers at institutions I'd never have had any reason to contact otherwise — people working on questions that intersect with my own in ways I wouldn't have discovered through a literature search alone. There's something incredibly powerful about being able to just reach out to someone whose paper you found fascinating and have them respond within hours, as opposed to the old model of hoping you both happen to attend the same conference. For early career researchers and PhD students especially, that kind of access is HUGE — we don't have the established networks that senior academics have built over decades, so social media genuinely levels the playing field in a way I find exciting. I've also found that interdisciplinary collaborations are much more likely to emerge organically through social media than through formal channels, because you start following someone's work out of genuine curiosity and a conversation develops naturally from there. The serendipity of it is something I really value — you cant engineer that kind of connection in an email cold-call, but Twitter somehow makes it feel natural and mutual. It's not just about exchanging contact details at a conference anymore; it's about building real, ongoing intellectual relationships with people who genuinely care about the same questions you do, and for someone doing a PhD who doesn't yet have a big name or a full publication list, that visibility and accessibility honestly makes an enormous difference.

Q63.text: Open access is the single biggest thing publishers could do, and I know that's not a new argument but it bears repeating because it is DIRECTLY relevant to social media usefulness — if I tweet about a paper and someone clicks through to a paywall, that conversation dies instantly. The whole point of reaching beyond the academic bubble collapses the second a curious member of the public hits a "subscribe for $35" screen. So making more content freely available, or at minimum providing a publicly accessible summary or lay abstract as standard, would transform what researchers can actually do with social media outreach. Beyond access, I'd love to see publishers invest in better sharing infrastructure — things like automatically generated tweet-length summaries, shareable visual abstracts, or even short video abstracts that researchers could post directly. Some journals are starting to do this and honestly it makes such a difference; you shouldn't need to be a graphic designer on top of everything else to communicate your work effectively online. I'd also really value some kind of altmetrics integration that's actually prominent and meaningful rather than a tiny badge buried in the sidebar — if you could see in real time that your paper had been discussed in 200 tweets or picked up by a science communicator with 50,000 followers, that would reinforce to researchers that this stuff MATTERS and encourage more of them to engage. Publishers have enormous reach and credibility, and I think they're leaving a lot on the table by not positioning themselves as active partners in public science communication rather than just gatekeepers of the final product. If they leaned into that role, it would benefit everyone — including their own visibility and relevance in a landscape that's changing really fast.

Q65.text: I just want to say that I think the academic community is at a genuine inflection point with social media, and I'm not sure everyone appreciates how much is at stake. The researchers who are still waiting on the sidelines, treating it as optional or slightly beneath them, are going to find themselves increasingly irrelevant to public discourse — not because the public doesn't care about their work, but because someone else will be there explaining it first, and not always accurately. That's actually what worries me MOST: the vacuum that disengaged researchers leave gets filled by people who may not have the expertise or the commitment to getting it right. Science communicators are doing incredible work but they cant be everywhere, and no one knows your research better than you do. So honestly my biggest takeaway from years of doing this alongside my PhD is that social media isn't a distraction from being a good researcher — it IS part of being a good researcher in 2017, full stop. I'd love to see that attitude shift institutionally, not just at the individual level. If universities and publishers and funding bodies started treating public engagement on social media as a legitimate measure of research impact rather than something you do in your spare time, I think you'd see a massive cultural change really quickly. The appetite is there on the public side — I see it every single day in the comments and shares and messages from people who are genuinely excited about science and just want someone to talk to them like an intelligent adult. We owe it to them, and honestly we owe it to ourselves, to show up and meet that appetite. I feel really lucky to have found that community early in my career and I hope this survey helps make the case for institutions to take it more seriously.
